sections.passage_title: The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete
sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete

Paragraph A: While modern Portland cement structures frequently deteriorate within fifty to one hundred years—especially when exposed to harsh maritime environments—ancient Roman piers, breakwaters, and monuments remain structurally sound after more than two millennia. Structures like the Pantheon in Rome, crowned by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the submerged harbor piers of Caesarea Maritima in the eastern Mediterranean continue to baffle modern materials scientists with their immense durability.

Paragraph B: Recent mineralogical investigations led by international geochemists have revealed the chemical secrets behind this extraordinary longevity. The Romans prepared their concrete (opus caementicium) by combining slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) with reactive volcanic ash known as pozzolana, obtained primarily from the Gulf of Naples. When mixed with volcanic rock aggregates (tuff) and seawater, this slurry initiated a slow, pozzolanic reaction that produced a dense calcium-aluminum-silicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) cementitious matrix.

Paragraph C: The most revolutionary discovery emerged from high-resolution synchrotron X-ray microdiffraction analysis of Roman maritime drill cores. Researchers discovered that when seawater percolates through microscopic pores in submerged Roman concrete, it dissolves residual lime clasts—small, unmixed white nodules of calcium oxide. The alkaline seawater then reacts with the volcanic ash to crystallize a rare, platy mineral called aluminous tobermorite (Al-tobermorite), interspersed with phillipsite crystals.

Paragraph D: In modern concrete, internal cracking typically leads to progressive structural failure as water rusts internal steel rebar. In contrast, the crystallization of Al-tobermorite inside Roman concrete acts as a dynamic self-healing mechanism. Instead of widening, micro-cracks provide channels through which percolating seawater triggers renewed crystal growth, interlocking adjacent cement grains and effectively reinforcing the structural matrix over centuries.

Paragraph E: Furthermore, hot-mixing techniques utilized by Roman master masons played a crucial role. Historical texts by the architect Vitruvius describe incorporating quicklime (unslaked calcium oxide) directly into the mix, producing high exothermic temperatures exceeding 200°C. This intense heat created brittle, reactive lime clast inclusions that dispersed evenly throughout the mortar, providing a ready reservoir of self-healing minerals across the entire monument.

Paragraph F: Today, materials engineers are actively translating these ancient Roman insights into low-carbon sustainable cements. Conventional Portland cement production is responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions due to high-temperature limestone kiln processing. By substituting industrial pozzolanic byproducts, such as coal fly ash and blast furnace slag, modern builders can produce self-healing maritime infrastructure while cutting greenhouse emissions by more than 40%.

sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

Paragraph F: The study of deep-sea bioluminescent proteins has revolutionized modern biotechnology. The discovery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and various luciferases has provided cell biologists with molecular beacons to track gene expression, tumor metastasis, and viral infections in real time. As robotic submersibles venture deeper into previously unexplored oceanic trenches, scientists continue to identify novel luminescent enzymes that promise breakthroughs in biomedical diagnostics.

READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.

READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

Paragraph F: The study of deep-sea bioluminescent proteins has revolutionized modern biotechnology. The discovery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and various luciferases has provided cell biologists with molecular beacons to track gene expression, tumor metastasis, and viral infections in real time. As robotic submersibles venture deeper into previously unexplored oceanic trenches, scientists continue to identify novel luminescent enzymes that promise breakthroughs in biomedical diagnostics.

READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.

sections.passage_title: The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete
sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete

Paragraph A: While modern Portland cement structures frequently deteriorate within fifty to one hundred years—especially when exposed to harsh maritime environments—ancient Roman piers, breakwaters, and monuments remain structurally sound after more than two millennia. Structures like the Pantheon in Rome, crowned by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the submerged harbor piers of Caesarea Maritima in the eastern Mediterranean continue to baffle modern materials scientists with their immense durability.

Paragraph B: Recent mineralogical investigations led by international geochemists have revealed the chemical secrets behind this extraordinary longevity. The Romans prepared their concrete (opus caementicium) by combining slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) with reactive volcanic ash known as pozzolana, obtained primarily from the Gulf of Naples. When mixed with volcanic rock aggregates (tuff) and seawater, this slurry initiated a slow, pozzolanic reaction that produced a dense calcium-aluminum-silicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) cementitious matrix.

Paragraph C: The most revolutionary discovery emerged from high-resolution synchrotron X-ray microdiffraction analysis of Roman maritime drill cores. Researchers discovered that when seawater percolates through microscopic pores in submerged Roman concrete, it dissolves residual lime clasts—small, unmixed white nodules of calcium oxide. The alkaline seawater then reacts with the volcanic ash to crystallize a rare, platy mineral called aluminous tobermorite (Al-tobermorite), interspersed with phillipsite crystals.

Paragraph D: In modern concrete, internal cracking typically leads to progressive structural failure as water rusts internal steel rebar. In contrast, the crystallization of Al-tobermorite inside Roman concrete acts as a dynamic self-healing mechanism. Instead of widening, micro-cracks provide channels through which percolating seawater triggers renewed crystal growth, interlocking adjacent cement grains and effectively reinforcing the structural matrix over centuries.

Paragraph E: Furthermore, hot-mixing techniques utilized by Roman master masons played a crucial role. Historical texts by the architect Vitruvius describe incorporating quicklime (unslaked calcium oxide) directly into the mix, producing high exothermic temperatures exceeding 200°C. This intense heat created brittle, reactive lime clast inclusions that dispersed evenly throughout the mortar, providing a ready reservoir of self-healing minerals across the entire monument.

Paragraph F: Today, materials engineers are actively translating these ancient Roman insights into low-carbon sustainable cements. Conventional Portland cement production is responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions due to high-temperature limestone kiln processing. By substituting industrial pozzolanic byproducts, such as coal fly ash and blast furnace slag, modern builders can produce self-healing maritime infrastructure while cutting greenhouse emissions by more than 40%.

READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.

sections.passage_title: The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete
sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete

Paragraph A: While modern Portland cement structures frequently deteriorate within fifty to one hundred years—especially when exposed to harsh maritime environments—ancient Roman piers, breakwaters, and monuments remain structurally sound after more than two millennia. Structures like the Pantheon in Rome, crowned by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the submerged harbor piers of Caesarea Maritima in the eastern Mediterranean continue to baffle modern materials scientists with their immense durability.

Paragraph B: Recent mineralogical investigations led by international geochemists have revealed the chemical secrets behind this extraordinary longevity. The Romans prepared their concrete (opus caementicium) by combining slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) with reactive volcanic ash known as pozzolana, obtained primarily from the Gulf of Naples. When mixed with volcanic rock aggregates (tuff) and seawater, this slurry initiated a slow, pozzolanic reaction that produced a dense calcium-aluminum-silicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) cementitious matrix.

Paragraph C: The most revolutionary discovery emerged from high-resolution synchrotron X-ray microdiffraction analysis of Roman maritime drill cores. Researchers discovered that when seawater percolates through microscopic pores in submerged Roman concrete, it dissolves residual lime clasts—small, unmixed white nodules of calcium oxide. The alkaline seawater then reacts with the volcanic ash to crystallize a rare, platy mineral called aluminous tobermorite (Al-tobermorite), interspersed with phillipsite crystals.

Paragraph D: In modern concrete, internal cracking typically leads to progressive structural failure as water rusts internal steel rebar. In contrast, the crystallization of Al-tobermorite inside Roman concrete acts as a dynamic self-healing mechanism. Instead of widening, micro-cracks provide channels through which percolating seawater triggers renewed crystal growth, interlocking adjacent cement grains and effectively reinforcing the structural matrix over centuries.

Paragraph E: Furthermore, hot-mixing techniques utilized by Roman master masons played a crucial role. Historical texts by the architect Vitruvius describe incorporating quicklime (unslaked calcium oxide) directly into the mix, producing high exothermic temperatures exceeding 200°C. This intense heat created brittle, reactive lime clast inclusions that dispersed evenly throughout the mortar, providing a ready reservoir of self-healing minerals across the entire monument.

Paragraph F: Today, materials engineers are actively translating these ancient Roman insights into low-carbon sustainable cements. Conventional Portland cement production is responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions due to high-temperature limestone kiln processing. By substituting industrial pozzolanic byproducts, such as coal fly ash and blast furnace slag, modern builders can produce self-healing maritime infrastructure while cutting greenhouse emissions by more than 40%.

sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

Paragraph F: The study of deep-sea bioluminescent proteins has revolutionized modern biotechnology. The discovery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and various luciferases has provided cell biologists with molecular beacons to track gene expression, tumor metastasis, and viral infections in real time. As robotic submersibles venture deeper into previously unexplored oceanic trenches, scientists continue to identify novel luminescent enzymes that promise breakthroughs in biomedical diagnostics.

sections.passage_title: The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete
sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete

Paragraph A: While modern Portland cement structures frequently deteriorate within fifty to one hundred years—especially when exposed to harsh maritime environments—ancient Roman piers, breakwaters, and monuments remain structurally sound after more than two millennia. Structures like the Pantheon in Rome, crowned by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the submerged harbor piers of Caesarea Maritima in the eastern Mediterranean continue to baffle modern materials scientists with their immense durability.

Paragraph B: Recent mineralogical investigations led by international geochemists have revealed the chemical secrets behind this extraordinary longevity. The Romans prepared their concrete (opus caementicium) by combining slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) with reactive volcanic ash known as pozzolana, obtained primarily from the Gulf of Naples. When mixed with volcanic rock aggregates (tuff) and seawater, this slurry initiated a slow, pozzolanic reaction that produced a dense calcium-aluminum-silicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) cementitious matrix.

Paragraph C: The most revolutionary discovery emerged from high-resolution synchrotron X-ray microdiffraction analysis of Roman maritime drill cores. Researchers discovered that when seawater percolates through microscopic pores in submerged Roman concrete, it dissolves residual lime clasts—small, unmixed white nodules of calcium oxide. The alkaline seawater then reacts with the volcanic ash to crystallize a rare, platy mineral called aluminous tobermorite (Al-tobermorite), interspersed with phillipsite crystals.

Paragraph D: In modern concrete, internal cracking typically leads to progressive structural failure as water rusts internal steel rebar. In contrast, the crystallization of Al-tobermorite inside Roman concrete acts as a dynamic self-healing mechanism. Instead of widening, micro-cracks provide channels through which percolating seawater triggers renewed crystal growth, interlocking adjacent cement grains and effectively reinforcing the structural matrix over centuries.

Paragraph E: Furthermore, hot-mixing techniques utilized by Roman master masons played a crucial role. Historical texts by the architect Vitruvius describe incorporating quicklime (unslaked calcium oxide) directly into the mix, producing high exothermic temperatures exceeding 200°C. This intense heat created brittle, reactive lime clast inclusions that dispersed evenly throughout the mortar, providing a ready reservoir of self-healing minerals across the entire monument.

Paragraph F: Today, materials engineers are actively translating these ancient Roman insights into low-carbon sustainable cements. Conventional Portland cement production is responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions due to high-temperature limestone kiln processing. By substituting industrial pozzolanic byproducts, such as coal fly ash and blast furnace slag, modern builders can produce self-healing maritime infrastructure while cutting greenhouse emissions by more than 40%.

sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

Paragraph F: The study of deep-sea bioluminescent proteins has revolutionized modern biotechnology. The discovery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and various luciferases has provided cell biologists with molecular beacons to track gene expression, tumor metastasis, and viral infections in real time. As robotic submersibles venture deeper into previously unexplored oceanic trenches, scientists continue to identify novel luminescent enzymes that promise breakthroughs in biomedical diagnostics.

READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.

READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.

sections.passage_title: The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete
sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete

Paragraph A: While modern Portland cement structures frequently deteriorate within fifty to one hundred years—especially when exposed to harsh maritime environments—ancient Roman piers, breakwaters, and monuments remain structurally sound after more than two millennia. Structures like the Pantheon in Rome, crowned by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the submerged harbor piers of Caesarea Maritima in the eastern Mediterranean continue to baffle modern materials scientists with their immense durability.

Paragraph B: Recent mineralogical investigations led by international geochemists have revealed the chemical secrets behind this extraordinary longevity. The Romans prepared their concrete (opus caementicium) by combining slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) with reactive volcanic ash known as pozzolana, obtained primarily from the Gulf of Naples. When mixed with volcanic rock aggregates (tuff) and seawater, this slurry initiated a slow, pozzolanic reaction that produced a dense calcium-aluminum-silicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) cementitious matrix.

Paragraph C: The most revolutionary discovery emerged from high-resolution synchrotron X-ray microdiffraction analysis of Roman maritime drill cores. Researchers discovered that when seawater percolates through microscopic pores in submerged Roman concrete, it dissolves residual lime clasts—small, unmixed white nodules of calcium oxide. The alkaline seawater then reacts with the volcanic ash to crystallize a rare, platy mineral called aluminous tobermorite (Al-tobermorite), interspersed with phillipsite crystals.

Paragraph D: In modern concrete, internal cracking typically leads to progressive structural failure as water rusts internal steel rebar. In contrast, the crystallization of Al-tobermorite inside Roman concrete acts as a dynamic self-healing mechanism. Instead of widening, micro-cracks provide channels through which percolating seawater triggers renewed crystal growth, interlocking adjacent cement grains and effectively reinforcing the structural matrix over centuries.

Paragraph E: Furthermore, hot-mixing techniques utilized by Roman master masons played a crucial role. Historical texts by the architect Vitruvius describe incorporating quicklime (unslaked calcium oxide) directly into the mix, producing high exothermic temperatures exceeding 200°C. This intense heat created brittle, reactive lime clast inclusions that dispersed evenly throughout the mortar, providing a ready reservoir of self-healing minerals across the entire monument.

Paragraph F: Today, materials engineers are actively translating these ancient Roman insights into low-carbon sustainable cements. Conventional Portland cement production is responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions due to high-temperature limestone kiln processing. By substituting industrial pozzolanic byproducts, such as coal fly ash and blast furnace slag, modern builders can produce self-healing maritime infrastructure while cutting greenhouse emissions by more than 40%.

READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.

sections.passage_title: The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete
sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete

Paragraph A: While modern Portland cement structures frequently deteriorate within fifty to one hundred years—especially when exposed to harsh maritime environments—ancient Roman piers, breakwaters, and monuments remain structurally sound after more than two millennia. Structures like the Pantheon in Rome, crowned by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the submerged harbor piers of Caesarea Maritima in the eastern Mediterranean continue to baffle modern materials scientists with their immense durability.

Paragraph B: Recent mineralogical investigations led by international geochemists have revealed the chemical secrets behind this extraordinary longevity. The Romans prepared their concrete (opus caementicium) by combining slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) with reactive volcanic ash known as pozzolana, obtained primarily from the Gulf of Naples. When mixed with volcanic rock aggregates (tuff) and seawater, this slurry initiated a slow, pozzolanic reaction that produced a dense calcium-aluminum-silicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) cementitious matrix.

Paragraph C: The most revolutionary discovery emerged from high-resolution synchrotron X-ray microdiffraction analysis of Roman maritime drill cores. Researchers discovered that when seawater percolates through microscopic pores in submerged Roman concrete, it dissolves residual lime clasts—small, unmixed white nodules of calcium oxide. The alkaline seawater then reacts with the volcanic ash to crystallize a rare, platy mineral called aluminous tobermorite (Al-tobermorite), interspersed with phillipsite crystals.

Paragraph D: In modern concrete, internal cracking typically leads to progressive structural failure as water rusts internal steel rebar. In contrast, the crystallization of Al-tobermorite inside Roman concrete acts as a dynamic self-healing mechanism. Instead of widening, micro-cracks provide channels through which percolating seawater triggers renewed crystal growth, interlocking adjacent cement grains and effectively reinforcing the structural matrix over centuries.

Paragraph E: Furthermore, hot-mixing techniques utilized by Roman master masons played a crucial role. Historical texts by the architect Vitruvius describe incorporating quicklime (unslaked calcium oxide) directly into the mix, producing high exothermic temperatures exceeding 200°C. This intense heat created brittle, reactive lime clast inclusions that dispersed evenly throughout the mortar, providing a ready reservoir of self-healing minerals across the entire monument.

Paragraph F: Today, materials engineers are actively translating these ancient Roman insights into low-carbon sustainable cements. Conventional Portland cement production is responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions due to high-temperature limestone kiln processing. By substituting industrial pozzolanic byproducts, such as coal fly ash and blast furnace slag, modern builders can produce self-healing maritime infrastructure while cutting greenhouse emissions by more than 40%.

READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

Paragraph F: The study of deep-sea bioluminescent proteins has revolutionized modern biotechnology. The discovery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and various luciferases has provided cell biologists with molecular beacons to track gene expression, tumor metastasis, and viral infections in real time. As robotic submersibles venture deeper into previously unexplored oceanic trenches, scientists continue to identify novel luminescent enzymes that promise breakthroughs in biomedical diagnostics.

sections.passage_title: The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete
sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

The Structural Secrets of Roman Concrete

Paragraph A: While modern Portland cement structures frequently deteriorate within fifty to one hundred years—especially when exposed to harsh maritime environments—ancient Roman piers, breakwaters, and monuments remain structurally sound after more than two millennia. Structures like the Pantheon in Rome, crowned by the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the submerged harbor piers of Caesarea Maritima in the eastern Mediterranean continue to baffle modern materials scientists with their immense durability.

Paragraph B: Recent mineralogical investigations led by international geochemists have revealed the chemical secrets behind this extraordinary longevity. The Romans prepared their concrete (opus caementicium) by combining slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) with reactive volcanic ash known as pozzolana, obtained primarily from the Gulf of Naples. When mixed with volcanic rock aggregates (tuff) and seawater, this slurry initiated a slow, pozzolanic reaction that produced a dense calcium-aluminum-silicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) cementitious matrix.

Paragraph C: The most revolutionary discovery emerged from high-resolution synchrotron X-ray microdiffraction analysis of Roman maritime drill cores. Researchers discovered that when seawater percolates through microscopic pores in submerged Roman concrete, it dissolves residual lime clasts—small, unmixed white nodules of calcium oxide. The alkaline seawater then reacts with the volcanic ash to crystallize a rare, platy mineral called aluminous tobermorite (Al-tobermorite), interspersed with phillipsite crystals.

Paragraph D: In modern concrete, internal cracking typically leads to progressive structural failure as water rusts internal steel rebar. In contrast, the crystallization of Al-tobermorite inside Roman concrete acts as a dynamic self-healing mechanism. Instead of widening, micro-cracks provide channels through which percolating seawater triggers renewed crystal growth, interlocking adjacent cement grains and effectively reinforcing the structural matrix over centuries.

Paragraph E: Furthermore, hot-mixing techniques utilized by Roman master masons played a crucial role. Historical texts by the architect Vitruvius describe incorporating quicklime (unslaked calcium oxide) directly into the mix, producing high exothermic temperatures exceeding 200°C. This intense heat created brittle, reactive lime clast inclusions that dispersed evenly throughout the mortar, providing a ready reservoir of self-healing minerals across the entire monument.

Paragraph F: Today, materials engineers are actively translating these ancient Roman insights into low-carbon sustainable cements. Conventional Portland cement production is responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions due to high-temperature limestone kiln processing. By substituting industrial pozzolanic byproducts, such as coal fly ash and blast furnace slag, modern builders can produce self-healing maritime infrastructure while cutting greenhouse emissions by more than 40%.

sections.passage_content:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

Paragraph F: The study of deep-sea bioluminescent proteins has revolutionized modern biotechnology. The discovery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and various luciferases has provided cell biologists with molecular beacons to track gene expression, tumor metastasis, and viral infections in real time. As robotic submersibles venture deeper into previously unexplored oceanic trenches, scientists continue to identify novel luminescent enzymes that promise breakthroughs in biomedical diagnostics.

READING PASSAGE 3

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.

READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Bioluminescence in the Abyssal Ocean

Paragraph A: Below the photic zone of the world's oceans, descending beyond 200 metres into the mesopelagic and bathypelagic realms, sunlight fades into complete obscurity. In this perpetual abyss—where temperatures hover near freezing and hydrostatic pressures exceed several hundred atmospheres—life thrives through the generation of biological light. Marine biologists estimate that over 75% of deep-sea organisms, spanning bacteria, cnidarians, cephalopods, and teleost fishes, possess bioluminescent capability.

Paragraph B: At its molecular foundation, bioluminescence is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent process. Unlike incandescent electrical bulbs, which waste up to 90% of energy as thermal heat, bioluminescence emits 'cold light', converting over 95% of chemical energy into visible photons. The reaction requires two primary biochemical agents: a substrate pigment known as luciferin, and a catalytic enzyme termed luciferase. In the presence of dissolved oxygen and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), luciferase oxidizes luciferin to form an excited oxyluciferin complex, which releases light upon relaxing to its ground state.

Paragraph C: Because red light wavelengths are rapidly absorbed by water in the first ten metres of the water column, the overwhelming majority of abyssal bioluminescence is emitted in the blue-green spectral band (470–490 nanometres). Blue-green photons travel farthest through seawater and correspond precisely to the visual pigments of bathypelagic predators. A notable exception is the dragonfish (genus Malacosteus), which produces far-red light from suborbital photophores. Because most deep-sea prey lack red photoreceptors, the dragonfish effectively possesses an invisible biological sniper beam.

Paragraph D: Deep-sea creatures exploit bioluminescence for a multifaceted suite of survival strategies. Counterillumination is perhaps the most widespread defensive mechanism. Hatchetfish and squids possess ventral photophores that emit downward-directed light matching the exact wavelength and intensity of residual downwelling sunlight, effectively erasing their silhouettes from upward-looking ambush predators. Conversely, dinoflagellates and jellyfish utilize bioluminescence as a 'burglar alarm': when disturbed by a grazer, they flash brightly to illuminate the predator, exposing it to higher-level apex hunters.

Paragraph E: Predatory lures represent another evolutionary masterpiece. The deep-sea anglerfish displays an esca—a bioluminescent bulb suspended from a modified dorsal ray. Within the esca, symbiotic phototrophic bacteria (Photobacterium) proliferate, producing an alluring glow that draws inquisitive crustaceans directly into the anglerfish's gaping maw. Similarly, the cookiecutter shark employs bioluminescence to camouflage its body while leaving a dark collar exposed, mimicking a small silhouette to entice larger tuna and swordfish before ambushing them.

Paragraph F: The study of deep-sea bioluminescent proteins has revolutionized modern biotechnology. READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

The Marvels of Urban Rewilding

Paragraph A: As global urban expansion accelerates, modern cities face severe environmental degradation, marked by the urban heat island effect, toxic air pollution, and catastrophic losses in biodiversity. In conventional metropolitan planning, asphalt pavements and concrete structures absorb solar radiation, raising urban temperatures by up to 5°C compared with surrounding rural hinterlands. In response to these pressing challenges, urban ecologists and landscape architects have pioneered 'urban rewilding'—an initiative to re-introduce native ecological systems, micro-wetlands, and continuous green corridors directly into city centres.

Paragraph B: Pioneering projects in cities like Singapore, Milan, and Seoul demonstrate that urban rewilding produces measurable microclimatic improvements. The integration of vertical forests, intensive living roofs, and naturalized drainage swales significantly boosts evapotranspiration, which cools surrounding air naturally. In Singapore's Parkroyal development, vegetative cover exceeds 200% of the site footprint. Measurements confirm that foliage intercepts up to 70% of direct solar radiation, while substrate soils act as acoustic dampening buffers, cutting ambient street traffic noise by up to eight decibels.

Paragraph C: Beyond temperature and acoustics, the restoration of native flora supports unexpected wildlife resilience. When London created a network of wildflower meadows across city roundabouts and disused rail embankments, entomologists recorded a 45% increase in native bumblebee diversity within three seasons. Similarly, rewilded wetlands along the Cheonggyecheon stream in Seoul provided vital stopover habitats for over thirty migratory bird species that had not been documented in the metropolitan basin for four decades.

Paragraph D: The psychological and cognitive dividends of accessible urban nature are equally well-documented. Epidemiological investigations conducted across European capitals show that residents living within 300 metres of biodiverse green corridors exhibit significantly lower baseline levels of cortisol—the primary human stress hormone. Clinical studies in biophilic workplace environments indicate a 15% increase in cognitive stamina and notable reductions in sick leave, illustrating that biological connectivity is essential for human well-being.

Paragraph E: Despite these compelling advantages, urban rewilding poses unique structural and regulatory hurdles. Retrofitting older high-rises with extensive soil substrates incurs substantial load-bearing penalties, necessitating structural reinforcements that can be cost-prohibitive. Furthermore, drainage systems must be engineered with multi-stage root barriers to prevent waterproofing membrane perforation. Horticulturalists must also choose drought-resilient native species to avoid straining municipal water reserves during arid summer heatwaves.

Paragraph F: Urban planners emphasize that rewilding must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought. Moving forward, municipal zoning laws are beginning to enforce biotope area ratios (BAR), mandating that all new civic developments allocate at least 30% of their surface footprint to permeable, ecologically functional greenery. By blending automated micro-irrigation with native planting strategies, cities of the twenty-first century can transition from concrete heat traps into vibrant, self-sustaining ecosystems.
